body_html:
Update:

  • Sep18’26: Q4 2026 Earnings Results

Back in my corporate finance days, we were always hunting for ways to save a penny—or two, if we got lucky. Especially at the 3G Capital-controlled companies I worked for, where cost-cutting was basically a core value. One of the classics? Offshoring repetitive, low-value work. I was all for it. I hated mind-numbing tasks, and offshoring was supposed to save money and free up my time. Win-win, right?

Not exactly. What we got back was ... rough. I spent more time double-checking than I would’ve spent doing the work myself. And since the idea was that offshoring would lighten my load, I ended up getting more responsibilities. So now I was redoing offshore work and juggling a bigger plate.

That was about 15 years ago. Offshoring has come a long way since then, mirroring broader shifts in the BPO (Business Process Outsourcing) industry where global talent quality has improved, integration tools have matured, and digital-first delivery models have become the norm. The talent pool is stronger, the teams are better educated, and integration with onshore operations has improved. But new issues emerged. The quality gap narrowed—but costs crept up. In one of my more recent roles, the supposed “savings” from offshoring were basically meaningless.

That’s when I really started digging into the BPO model. I realized that while some companies get it wrong—throwing bodies at a problem and calling it strategy—others get it very, very right. This deep dive isn’t a how-to manual for optimizing your offshore team (though I’m happy to chat if you're into that). Instead, it’s about a small BPO company that’s nailing the execution, and whose stock looks like a compelling investment.

Why this BPO investing opportunity stands out

When a “boring” call center outsourcer starts printing record revenue, expanding margins, and buys back nearly a fifth of its shares overnight, it’s time to pay attention. This company is a mid-cap CX (customer experience) provider flying under the radar, even as it transforms its business in plain sight. It’s operating in a segment of BPO that’s benefiting from two undeniable trends: offshore labour efficiency and AI-driven customer service.

Despite a solid track record and improving fundamentals, the stock trades at just 5.3x EBITDA and 12.2x earnings—a discount to both peers and reality. With a target price that implies 160% upside, this company’s high-margin, tech-enabled model and recent strategic moves make it one of the more interesting compounders hiding in plain sight.

In this deep dive, we’ll unpack one of the most interesting compounders hiding in plain sight.

Let’s dive in 🤿!

This deep dive is +6,500 words long, so below is a table of contents if you are interested in a specific topic.

  • How IBEX wins in offshore BPO and customer experience outsourcing

  • IBEX’s tech edge: AI-powered CX and the Wave iX platform

  • A Quick Look Back: The Origins of IBEX

  • Margin Expansion: A Profitable Shift to Offshore + Tech

  • Revving Up Revenue: New Wins and Fading Legacy Drags

  • Share Buybacks: Management Skin in the Game (EPS Booster)

  • Competition and Valuation: Undervalued vs. Peers

  • Key Risks to the Thesis

  • Valuation: Undervalued CX Stock With 160% Upside

  • Conclusion: High-Conviction Upside in an Overlooked Gem

How IBEX wins in offshore BPO and customer experience outsourcing

BPO is all about companies handing off non-core tasks—like customer service or tech support—to specialized third-party providers. The idea is simple: outsourcing saves money and lets companies focus on what they do best. BPO providers run call centers and digital service hubs to handle customer interactions on behalf of clients, often more efficiently (and cheaply) than the client could on its own. Crucially, where those service centers are located makes a big difference:

  • Onshore BPO means the work is done domestically (e.g., a US company outsourcing to a US-based call center). This can offer closer cultural alignment and time-zone convenience, but it costs more due to higher local wages.

  • Offshore BPO sends the work overseas (think customer support from the Philippines or Pakistan). Labour costs are far lower, so offshoring dramatically cuts expenses—albeit with potential language or cultural gaps. Many companies find the savings well worth it, especially as global talent and technology improve the quality of service.

IBEX has fully embraced offshore BPO. Over the last few years, it shifted nearly all of its operations to lower-cost countries. As of mid-2024, 95% of IBEX’s delivery center capacity is located in high-growth, high-margin nearshore/offshore markets (Philippines, Jamaica, Nicaragua, Pakistan, etc.), up from ~50% just a few years ago.

The result? IBEX provides the same services at a lower cost, boosting profit margins. Work done offshore or nearshore simply generates higher margins than onshore work. By shifting more volume abroad, IBEX has cut expenses and improved profitability, even while trimming some low-margin domestic revenue.

This broader industry shift toward offshore BPO has only accelerated as companies seek cost efficiencies and global reach. In its 10-Q filing (page 25), IBEX’s management noted that, “Clients and prospective clients look to relocate work to cost advantageous markets in the near term.” And IBEX is ready—it’s already built extra offshore capacity to meet this growing demand.

Even amid macroeconomic volatility, demand for customer experience outsourcing remains strong. Companies still need to support customers—and many prefer outsourcing to save money and gain operational flexibility, especially when technology adds value.

Speaking of tech, cost arbitrage isn’t IBEX’s only trick. The company is transforming itself from a traditional call center into a digital-first CX provider, blending human agents with AI and analytics. That brings us to IBEX’s secret sauce: its tech stack and innovative platform.

IBEX’s tech edge: AI-powered CX and the Wave iX platform

If the word “outsourcing” makes you think of massive call centers filled with headsets and hold music, you’re not wrong — but IBEX is far from a commodity call-center shop. The company has intentionally built a differentiated, tech-driven business model to stand out in the crowded BPO field. At the heart of this strategy is IBEX’s proprietary Wave iX platform.

What is Wave iX? It’s IBEX’s in-house suite of digital solutions and AI tools that supercharge the standard customer service offering. Think of it as an “automation and intelligence overlay” on top of the thousands of agents IBEX employs. According to the company, Wave iX (an evolution of their prior WaveX platform) is designed to “power enhanced agent interactions, exceptional client CX, and overall better performance.” In practice, this means IBEX isn’t just renting out call center workers; it’s also selling software and tech-driven processes that make those workers more effective and the client’s customers happier.

Tangible examples of Wave iX in action

AI-Powered Translation

IBEX has developed real-time translation tech that allows an English-speaking agent to support customers in multiple languages. This is game-changing for global companies. Instead of hiring separate teams for Spanish, French, etc., a single IBEX agent (with Wave iX AI) can serve all those customers on the fly. One IBEX hospitality client now uses English-speaking agents with AI translators to handle multilingual callers – no more awkward hand-offs or long holds waiting for a specialist. The outcome is not just cost savings (fewer total agents needed) but also a smoother customer experience. IBEX is basically displacing old-school translation service bureaus with this AI translator solution, and it’s 100% accretive to revenue and profit since it’s a premium service clients pay extra for.

AI Automation (“Bots”)

IBEX’s platform also offers AI-driven chatbots and voice bots that can automate low-level customer inquiries. Rather than view automation as a threat (if a bot handles calls, do we need agents?), IBEX turned it into a revenue opportunity. The company provides “AI Automated Solutions” to clients, handling the simple, high-volume calls through bots, while human agents tackle the complex issues. In many client engagements, IBEX is one of multiple BPO vendors serving a company, and IBEX has uniquely positioned itself to manage 100% of the automated interactions across all vendors. That means IBEX gets an incremental slice of work (and profit) by running the automation layer, on top of its share of live agents. It also deepens IBEX’s integration with the client (harder to rip out), effectively expanding its moat by being the go-to AI partner.

Analytics & Omnichannel

Beyond AI, Wave iX includes analytics tools that crunch interaction data to glean customer insights, plus an omnichannel platform to seamlessly handle contacts via phone, email, chat, SMS, and social media. For clients, this means IBEX isn’t just a people provider but a tech-enabled consultant helping improve customer satisfaction scores and sales conversion.

All of this tech focus has shifted IBEX’s value prop from pure “we have cheaper agents” to “we drive better customer experiences with fewer headaches.” Management highlights that they’ve “transformed our business from a traditional BPO of commoditized call center support to a technology-led provider”. That’s a bold claim, but the evidence is there: IBEX has invested heavily in proprietary software and integrated third-party AI solutions into its offerings. By bringing these to clients early, IBEX aims to capture the upside of AI-driven work rather than get disrupted by it – essentially future-proofing its revenue stream.

It’s working. IBEX’s differentiated approach is helping win “large enterprise deals with trophy brands”. New clients are choosing IBEX because of its tech capabilities (like Wave iX) on top of reliable service. And existing clients are sticking around — IBEX boasts revenue retention rates among the highest in the industry. During the Q2 2025 earnings call, the CEO said:

Also important to our success is our high client retention where our revenue retention rates are some of the highest in the industry, highlighting our ability to be a strategic partner with our clients.

In short, IBEX isn’t competing on lowest cost alone; it’s competing on value. That shows up in its financial performance, especially on the margin side.

A Quick Look Back: The Origins of IBEX

IBEX Limited traces its roots to The Resource Group International Limited (TRGI), a private investment and operations firm. Incorporated in Bermuda, IBEX was established to consolidate and expand TRGI's CX and BPO operations. Over the years, IBEX evolved from a traditional call center operator into a tech-enabled CX partner, leveraging digital engagement tools and a global delivery footprint.

The company went public on the NASDAQ on August 7, 2020. The IPO involved the sale of 3,571,429 common shares by IBEX and 1,190,476 common shares by its majority shareholder, TRGI, for $19.00 per share.

The IPO proceeds were utilized to strengthen IBEX's balance sheet and support its growth initiatives, particularly in expanding its digital CX capabilities and global delivery centers. Post-IPO, IBEX has focused on diversifying its client base across various verticals, including retail, healthtech, fintech, and utilities, while investing in technology-driven solutions like its Wave iX platform to enhance customer engagement and operational efficiency.

TRGI remained IBEX’s majority shareholder for several years, but that changed in November 2024, when IBEX repurchased 3.56 million shares from TRGI at $19.65 per share, effectively ending TRGI’s majority control. As partial payment, IBEX issued TRGI a convertible promissory note, which allows TRGI to convert the note into up to ~1.9 million IBEX shares starting in late 2025, at a price between $13.10 and $19.65 per share, depending on market conditions.

Following the repurchase, TRGI's direct ownership dropped to 13.1%, eliminating its majority control and ending IBEX’s “controlled company” status. However, Zia Chishti, TRGI’s founder and former chairman, continues to hold an additional 5.2% of IBEX shares personally (682,318 shares), bringing the combined influence of TRGI and Chishti to roughly 18.3%. While TRGI no longer has formal control, this combined stake still gives the original backers meaningful influence. That said, with an independent board now in place and no controlling shareholder, the governance profile is significantly improved, removing a key overhang for institutional investors.

Margin Expansion: A Profitable Shift to Offshore + Tech

One of the most compelling parts of the IBEX story is margin expansion. This company has steadily improved its profitability over the past few years, thanks to the strategic choices we discussed (offshore mix + tech overlay).

Offshore Mix & Site Optimization

As noted, IBEX generates higher margins from offshore operations than U.S. onshore work. By growing its offshore capacity and closing or shrinking expensive onshore sites, IBEX has structurally lifted its gross and operating margins. In fiscal 2024, management deliberately pruned some low-margin revenue in the U.S. to focus on higher-margin offshore business — a move that temporarily dampened sales growth but boosted profitability. Now ~95% of its seats are in cheaper locales, so the heavy lifting is done. The ongoing benefit is that each dollar of revenue now carries a higher profit percentage.

For example, when IBEX adds a new client program, odds are it’s being serviced out of Jamaica or the Philippines (rather than, say, Texas), meaning better margins out of the gate. In Q2 FY2025, IBEX’s offshore revenue grew 14% YoY – that’s in their highest-margin region, so it helped push EBITDA margins up by 100 basis points year-over-year.

Capacity Utilization

Running large delivery centers comes with fixed costs (rent, management, infrastructure). The more “seats” you fill with revenue-generating agents, the more those fixed costs get covered. IBEX has been filling up its centers, driving utilization higher, especially offshore. This directly boosts operating margins: higher utilization = more revenue to cover fixed overhead.

During the six months ended Dec 2024, IBEX added capacity offshore and expected it to be absorbed quickly as clients shift work to cheaper locations. That’s exactly what’s happening. In short, IBEX now has a cost-efficient footprint and enough business to keep it buzzing, which yields nice operating leverage on each incremental contract.

Pricing Power (COLA Adjustments)

BPO contracts often include clauses for cost-of-living adjustments (COLA) or inflation pass-throughs. With global wages rising, IBEX has leaned on these contract features to raise prices for clients and offset wage inflation.

In fiscal 2024, the company successfully implemented higher client pricing under COLA provisions to counteract agent pay increases. This is a quiet but significant tailwind — not every industry can pass on inflation so readily. IBEX effectively protected its margins even as it gave raises to staff by telling clients, “Hey, our costs are up X%, per our agreement, your rates will go up X%.” That helped keep labour cost pressures from denting profit too much.

Additionally, IBEX improved agent retention and productivity, which also mitigated the impact of wage hikes (experienced agents handle calls faster and better, lowering the cost per interaction).

Efficiency and Scale

As IBEX grows, some expenses don’t grow with it. G&A costs as a percentage of revenue can fall, procurement gets bulk discounts, and the company can automate more internal processes. There’s a bit of economies of scale for a mid-sized player like IBEX — it’s not huge, but even slight reductions in overhead rate help margins. Management also credits operational improvements for margin gains, like better hiring/training (reducing costly attrition) and leveraging analytics to streamline workflows.

Importantly, these factors are showing up in the numbers. In Q2 FY2025, IBEX’s adjusted EBITDA margin hit 11.8%, up from 10.8% a year prior.

EBITDA margin and net margin have been on an upward trend and are at multi-year highs — an impressive streak in an industry known for thin margins.

Its ROE and ROIC are also exceptionally high. This profitability profile suggests IBEX’s strategy is yielding more than just growth – it’s yielding profitable growth.

And the best part? There are still margin drivers ahead. As new AI services ramp up, they should carry high margins (software-like economics). Further site optimization in high-cost areas (IBEX still has ~5% onshore capacity, it could trim, and continued COLA pricing actions can add incremental basis points. Management remains confident that margins can keep expanding alongside revenue, as mentioned during the Q2 2025 earnings call:

These vectors have enabled us to expand adjusted EBITDA margin consistently. As a result, we remain confident in our ability to continue to drive top line growth and expand margin.

Speaking of revenue, let’s examine IBEX’s growth trajectory, which is poised to accelerate as some past headwinds fade away.

Revving Up Revenue: New Wins and Fading Legacy Drags

IBEX’s revenue growth story has two sides: headwinds from legacy business that are diminishing, and tailwinds from new clients and vertical expansion that are strengthening. The net result is that growth is picking up after a sluggish period.

First, the headwinds: In the last year or two, IBEX’s top line was held back by a decline in its FinTech client segment and the intentional wind-down of low-margin programs. For example, in Q2 FY2025, IBEX’s exposure to the FinTech vertical (think online finance apps, fintech startups, etc.) fell to 11% of revenue from 13.7% a year prior. Management cited a changing landscape in some fintech client support models — in plain English, some fintech clients hit turbulence and cut back on outsourcing volumes. This dragged on IBEX’s overall growth, since other segments had to counteract the loss. The good news is that FinTech is now a much smaller piece of the pie (just 11%), so even if it continues to struggle, its ability to weigh down overall growth is limited. In other key verticals, IBEX is actually growing nicely (more on that in a moment).

Another drag was IBEX’s deliberate shrinkage of onshore business as part of its margin strategy. The company essentially said, “We’re not going to chase low-margin domestic revenue just to show growth.” This meant letting some legacy contracts or sites in the U.S. go, causing a short-term dip in revenue. Indeed, management acknowledged that improvements in profitability “came at the cost of lower revenues, mainly due to a larger focus on higher margin offshore operations”. Now that this transition is largely done (the revenue mix is ~95% offshore/nearshore), IBEX can return to growth without that self-imposed handicap.

This feels like déjà vu. Remember Celestica? It also made the tough call to wind down its low-margin Cisco business and pivot toward higher-margin segments. We all saw how that turned out. Strategic pruning may look painful in the short term, but it’s often what sets the stage for a stronger, more profitable growth runway.

I am still bullish on Celestica. Read the deep dive if you forgot why I am bullish on the name.

Back to IBEX.

Turns out, pruning low-margin revenue works—just ask Q2. IBEX just notched its highest quarterly revenue ever in Q2, at $140.7 million (up 6.1% y/y). That 6.1% growth may not sound explosive, but it’s the fastest growth IBEX has posted in the past nine quarters.

In other words, the trend has increased upward. Management even raised their full-year 2025 revenue outlook to $525–$535 million (from a prior $515–$525M), signalling that things are coming in better than expected.

With the legacy drags fading, IBEX’s underlying growth engines are finally showing through.

Now those growth tailwinds:

New Client Wins (“New Logos”)

IBEX has been landing new customers, and importantly, big ones. In the latest quarter alone, it closed 5 new client deals, bringing the year-to-date total to 8 new logos. Winning new clients is vital for a BPO — it’s fresh revenue that can scale over time. IBEX has a strong “land and expand” track record: historically, a new client’s revenue grows 2.5x to 3x by the second or third year of the engagement as IBEX wins more of that client’s business. This means those 8 new wins in FY2025 could be worth two or three times their initial contract size by 2026-2027, fueling future growth.

Notably, IBEX is securing marquee brands (they mention “trophy brands” in enterprise deals, which not only bring revenue but also bolster IBEX’s credibility to win others in the same industry.

Expansion in Key Verticals

IBEX is seeing robust growth in certain industries it serves. HealthTech, Travel/Logistics, and Retail/e-Commerce are standouts. HealthTech revenue was up 31% y/y in Q2, and Travel/Transportation & Logistics up ~17%. These verticals now make up bigger portions of the mix (e.g. HealthTech 15.1% of rev, up from 12.2%).

What’s driving this is a mix of new client wins in those verticals and increased volume from existing clients (some of IBEX’s large tech and retail clients have grown their business with IBEX). As these fast-growing verticals become a larger share, they lift overall growth. Meanwhile, IBEX’s largest segment, Retail/e-Commerce (28.5% of rev), held even in a tough macro environment— a positive sign.

Existing Client Growth (Share Gains)

IBEX doesn’t just rely on signing new logos; it also grows by doing more for current clients. The company often starts with a small slice of a client’s support work and, by outperforming other vendors, wins a larger share of the pie (“share shift”). Clients reward the best-performing BPO with more volumes or additional lines of business.

IBEX has benefited from this dynamic, as reflected in its high retention and expanding engagements. IBEX bragged that one of its big wins from 2024 already became a top-20 client in 2025, evidence of successful land-and-expand. This organic growth within the base provides a steady underpinning to revenue.

Digital-First Demand

Broader industry trends are also favourable. Companies are investing in “digital-first” customer experience solutions, an area where IBEX is strong. IBEX noted that demand in the latest half-year was higher, partly due to increased demand for its digital-first CX solutions and new wins in strategic verticals. In other words, the market is looking for exactly what IBEX is selling— omnichannel support, AI integration, etc., not just vanilla call centers. This should help IBEX win its fair share of new contracts going forward.

Considering all these factors, I expect IBEX’s revenue growth to improve. Management’s confidence was evident in raising guidance. If FinTech stabilizes and the new client ramps kick in, there’s a chance IBEX could surprise to the upside on top-line growth. The “legacy drag” is largely in the rear-view mirror, and the road ahead is clearer.

Before moving to valuation, we have to talk about one more element of the thesis: IBEX’s capital allocation and recent aggressive share buybacks, which have turbocharged EPS and demonstrate management’s confidence.

Share Buybacks: Management Skin in the Game (EPS Booster)

It’s not often you see a company of IBEX’s size make dramatic moves with its share count, but IBEX’s board and management have been highly active in repurchasing stock since mid-2023— a bullish signal about how undervalued they believe it is.

There are two big pieces to this:

Ongoing Share Repurchase Program

In fiscal 2024, IBEX quietly bought back 1.3 million shares for $21.7 million. That amounted to roughly 8% of the outstanding shares, a meaningful reduction. This wasn’t just a one-off; it’s part of an authorized program to return capital to shareholders. Even after spending $21.7 million, the company had $27 million remaining under its repurchase authorization as of late 2024. The timing is noteworthy — IBEX’s stock had fallen over 50% from early 2023 highs, and management clearly saw a bargain. By buying back stock at depressed prices, they increased each remaining share’s claim on earnings (boosting EPS) and signalled confidence in the business.

Major Buyback from Controlling Shareholder (TRGI)

The biggest splash came in Q2 FY2025. IBEX executed a $70 million share repurchase deal with its largest shareholder, The Resource Group International (TRGI). IBEX bought ~3.6 million shares from TRGI, which was about 21% of the company’s outstanding shares! This one move shrank the share count by over one-fifth in a flash. It also had the side effect of freeing IBEX from “controlled company” status – TRGI’s stake dropped from majority control to around 13% (1.7 million shares remaining) after the deal.

For shareholders, this is a win-win: IBEX is now under standard NASDAQ governance (more independent board oversight) and those 3.6 million shares are essentially “retired.” The immediate impact was a 36% jump in adjusted EPS in Q2 YoY, partly attributable to having far fewer shares in the denominator. In fact, IBEX reported adjusted EPS of $0.59 for Q2, up from $0.44 a year prior, with the buyback amplifying the earnings growth. Management also raised full-year earnings guidance after the repurchase.

These buybacks demonstrate a few things. Firstly, management’s conviction: they are putting cash (and even new debt) to work because they truly believe IBEX stock is undervalued. (They even took on a $25 million convertible note and used a credit line to help fund the $70 million buyback— a bold move, essentially leveraging up to repurchase shares). While that does add some debt to the balance sheet, IBEX’s debt levels remain moderate and manageable, with net debt around $74 million post-deal (for context, annual EBITDA is ~$66 million, so net debt/EBITDA is ~1.1x).

Secondly, the buybacks have significantly improved IBEX’s per-share metrics and ownership structure. With ~13.2 million shares now outstanding (down from ~18 million in mid-2023), every dollar of profit is split into fewer pieces. If IBEX earns, say, $2.12 in adjusted EPS (the current TTM run-rate), a similar company with 18 million shares would only show ~$1.55 EPS — so IBEX’s EPS looks much better. This can lead to multiple expansion if the market recognizes the higher EPS and applies a normal P/E. It’s also a bit of a self-fulfilling boost to future EPS growth rates, since the share count is lower.

And importantly, removing the controlling shareholder overhang opens IBEX up to a broader investor base. Some institutional investors shy away from “controlled companies” due to governance concerns. Now IBEX has a fully independent board (they added new directors with strong industry and AI backgrounds as part of the change and could attract more interest.

In sum, IBEX’s capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly. They generate solid free cash flow and have chosen to give a chunk of it back via buybacks— a strong sign they believe the best investment is their own stock. Management still has authorization to buy more, and we wouldn’t be surprised to see additional repurchases given the remaining $27 million authorization and ongoing cash generation.

With operations humming, margins expanding, and management actively betting on the stock, why is IBEX still so cheap? Let’s compare it to some competitors and see how the market might be mispricing it.

Competition and Valuation: Undervalued vs. Peers

IBEX operates in a competitive landscape alongside other outsourced customer experience providers. Peers include TaskUs (TASK), TTEC Holdings (TTEC), and Concentrix (CNXC) (and to an extent giants like Teleperformance or Tech Mahindra’s BPO division, though those are much larger). Comparing IBEX to its peers on margins, growth, and valuation highlights just how attractive IBEX looks.

Margins, Growth & Balance Sheet Health

Among mid-sized CX outsourcing companies, IBEX’s EBITDA margin is lower than TASK’s and TTEC’s.

TASK is often considered a high-tech, digital-focused BPO (serving fast-growing tech companies, content moderation for social media, etc.). TTEC is a more traditional competitor with both customer care and digital consulting segments. While TASK is doing okay, TTEC has hit a rough patch: 2024 revenue fell ~10% amid client churn, and adjusted EBITDA margins dipped to ~9%. TTEC’s operating margin is only 4.1% as of Q4 2024, well below IBEX’s 8.5% and TASK’s 10.9%.

Plus, TTEC carries a lot of debt (nearly ~$1 billion net debt, almost 5x EBITDA!), which constrains its flexibility.

In contrast, TASK has net debt of 0.7x EBITDA and IBEX has net debt of 1.1x EBITDA. Essentially, IBEX outclasses TTEC on growth, margins and balance sheet health. TTEC’s struggles may be company-specific, but it shows that IBEX’s execution has put it in a leadership position among smaller BPOs.

Concentrix is a behemoth relative to IBEX, with $9.6 billion in revenue in 2024, ~19 times those of IBEX. Concentrix grew 35% in 2024, mainly due to the Webhelp merger; on a pro forma basis, organic growth was only ~2.7%. Its margins are decent at ~14% EBITDA margin and ~8% operating margin post-merger, but not wildly different from IBEX’s in percentage terms.

After reading the above, you may wonder why I bought IBEX rather than TASK, as the latter has better margins and a stronger balance sheet.

The answer is valuation and outlook, both of which I discuss in the next section.

Valuation Metrics

Now, valuation metrics for IBEX versus these peers:

EV/EBITDA

IBEX is trading around 5.3x TTM EV/EBITDA at current prices – this is well below TaskUs (8.2x) and even a hair below Concentrix (5.9x).

The sector median EV/EBITDA for similar companies is much higher, around 12.7x— in other words, IBEX is trading 50% below the sector median valuation multiple. Even if you forget valuation relative to peers, IBEX is trading below its 5-year historical multiple of 8.1x, even though margins and revenue are at an all-time high.

In plainer terms, IBEX is dirt cheap for its earnings level. Such a discount might be partially explained by its smaller size and lower liquidity, but it appears excessive given IBEX’s growth and margin profile.

P/E and PEG

IBEX trades around 12.2x trailing earnings. For comparison, Concentrix and TaskUs trade at higher P/Es of 12.7x and 27.2x, respectively.

And note, IBEX’s EPS growth has been stellar— 37% YoY in the recent quarter, 38% annually over the last 3 years and 14% forward EPS. So a low P/E in the face of high growth means a PEG ratio well below 1.

So while IBEX is trading around half of TASK on a P/E basis, if you adjust for the growth, IBEX is trading at one-tenth of TASK’s multiple. The market seems to be pricing IBEX as if its earnings might decline, which doesn’t square with the outlook.

As per Concentrix, because it is so large and slower-growing, its stock currently trades at a low valuation (5.9× EV/EBITDA). This provides context: the entire sector is valued on the cheap side right now, possibly due to investor fears around cyclicality or AI disruption.

Why is the market discounting IBEX? Possibly due to perceived risks — let’s address those directly, and see if they are manageable.

Key Risks to the Thesis

Client Concentration

Like many BPOs, IBEX relies on a handful of big clients for a large portion of revenue. Its top 5 clients account for 39% of revenue, and the top 10 about 54%. The largest single client is 12%. Losing or reducing business with any of these whales could sting.

This risk is somewhat mitigated by IBEX’s excellent client retention and deepening ties (it’s hard for a client to rip out a vendor that is performing well, and IBEX often embeds via tech services, which adds stickiness).

Also, concentration is improving as IBEX adds new customers – eight new clients in the first half of FY25 alone. Over time, new logos can diversify the base. On the flip side, IBEX’s strong execution has sometimes led clients to consolidate toward IBEX at the expense of others, but I can’t assume that always holds.

Automation and AI Disruption

The very AI technology that IBEX is embracing is, in a sense, a double-edged sword for the whole industry. If AI-driven bots get too good, companies might need far fewer human agents, shrinking the overall BPO opportunity. There is a risk that in a few years, customer service staffing needs could flatten or decline as algorithms handle more queries.

IBEX is tackling this by being a first-mover in offering AI solutions itself, aiming to capture AI-related work rather than lose it. They believe that by staying at the forefront, they can maintain and even grow revenue as the mix shifts to AI-enabled services.

So far, IBEX’s approach seems savvy, selling AI as a product. But it’s a risk if competitors leapfrog IBEX in AI, or if clients decide to develop their own in-house AI and cut out third parties. We saw IBEX’s Wave iX wins in translation and automation; those are encouraging.

The risk is more macro: could AI shrink the BPO market pie? In a bear scenario, yes, over a long horizon. Over the next few years, though, AI is likely to augment humans more than replace them in complex interactions, and IBEX will profit from that augmentation. This risk is real but not likely to materially derail IBEX in the near term.

Client Vendor Consolidation

Large enterprises often use multiple BPO vendors. There’s a trend in some cases to consolidate vendors to get better pricing or simplicity. If one of IBEX’s big clients decided to trim down to one partner, and IBEX didn’t make the cut, that would hurt. IBEX’s strategy to mitigate this is to be the highest performing vendor so that if consolidation happens, IBEX wins the bulk of the work rather than losing it.

They’ve cited examples of outperforming competitors and gaining share as a result. Still, being a mid-sized player, IBEX faces competition from giants like Teleperformance or Concentrix for global deals. There is also industry consolidation via M&A — competitors merging (as Concentrix did with Webhelp) —though IBEX itself could even be an attractive acquisition target someday, given its niche strengths.

Economic Cyclicality

IBEX’s fortunes are somewhat tied to its clients’ business volumes. If we hit a recession or one of IBEX’s key sectors (say e-commerce or travel) slumps, call volumes might drop or clients might tighten budgets, resulting in lower revenue for IBEX.

The BPO industry can experience short-term volatility based on client activity. For instance, if a retail client has fewer sales, they have fewer customer support calls, so they need fewer IBEX agents. The flip side is that during downturns, companies might actually outsource more to save costs. IBEX noted that overall demand in recent quarters has been solid despite macro headwinds. But it’s something to watch: a broad economic decline could slow IBEX’s growth temporarily.

Geopolitical/Operational Risks

Running operations in countries like the Philippines, Nicaragua, Jamaica, and Pakistan comes with certain risks — political instability, regulatory changes, currency fluctuations, etc. Any disruption (natural disasters, changes in labour law, etc.) in a key delivery country could impact IBEX’s service delivery or costs.

Additionally, IBEX is incorporated in Bermuda, which means some legal protections differ from a U.S. corporation (for example, certain shareholder rights or the enforceability of U.S. judgments). These are fairly standard risks for a global BPO, and IBEX has managed them for years.

Overall, IBEX’s risks are identifiable and manageable. The company has actively addressed many of them (diversifying clients, embracing AI, keeping the balance sheet prudent). No single client or technology appears likely to knock the company off course in the near term, and the biggest structural risk (AI) is something IBEX is turning into an opportunity. With risks accounted for, let’s circle back to valuation and what kind of upside scenario we’re looking at.

Valuation: Undervalued CX Stock With 160% Upside

My target value is $67 per share, which is +160% up from the current price. This value is conservative (as I will explain below), and in the worst case, I would see the shares trading at $13.50, which is 3.5 times EBITDA. This would imply an attractive risk-reward of 1:3.4.

I came up with a $67 value using a DCF model and a cost of capital of 7.2%. The cost of capital is based on:

  • a beta of 0.9

  • a long-term debt to capital ratio of 40%. While, the ratio has dropped below 40% in the last five years, I expect management to eventually optimize the capital structure by repurchasing shares or starting a dividend plan.

Below are the key financial assumptions.

I assume a revenue growth rate of 5%, which is very conservative. The CX BPO market—the segment IBEX actually plays in—is expected to grow at 11.6% annually through 2030, driven by digital-first demand, AI integration, and rising complexity in customer interactions.

In other words, this isn’t the flat, commoditized BPO segment people dismiss—it’s a part of the market that’s growing faster than many assume. Still, I’m assuming IBEX will grow slower than the industry and lose some share to larger players with deeper sales channels and scale advantages. But if IBEX simply maintains its current share, the implied valuation could push above $95 per share. And if it does what it’s already shown it can—win business away from slower competitors—then upside would be even higher.

We've seen above that IBEX has consistently taken share via new client wins, deeper wallet penetration, and a more compelling digital/AI overlay. But to play it safe, I’m modelling it like an underdog—even though its recent execution says otherwise.

As per margins, I kept them close to last year even though there are four strong drivers for expansion:

  • The continued shift to offshore delivery, where margins are structurally higher.

  • Increased utilization of existing capacity, which boosts operating leverage with minimal incremental cost.

  • COLA-driven pricing adjustments that pass through wage inflation to clients.

  • The ramp-up of high-margin AI-led services through Wave iX, like real-time translation and automation layers.

Still, I prefer to play it safe. There are real risks of margin compression:

  • Labour inflation could outpace COLA clauses.

  • Investment in automation might require near-term spending.

  • Vendor consolidation could pressure pricing, and some drag from legacy business might persist.

That said, most of these headwinds are either already accounted for or fading, while the tailwinds have only begun to play out.

Let’s address the elephant in the room: at $67 per share, IBEX would be trading at 25.5x earnings and 13.8x EBITDA. That P/E is still slightly below TASK’s 27x, but the EV/EBITDA multiple would actually be well above TASK’s 8x. So, I don’t expect the upside to come from multiple expansion alone. Instead, the stock should appreciate as IBEX delivers higher revenues and expanding margins. In other words, the lift will be driven more by a bigger denominator in the valuation ratios—EBITDA and earnings growing—than by a major re-rating. That’s why I see the share price climbing gradually, mostly around earnings releases as results come in stronger than expected.

Conclusion: High-Conviction Upside in an Overlooked Gem

IBEX Limited may not be a household name, but it checks a lot of boxes for a compelling investment: rising revenues, expanding margins, shareholder-friendly management, and a dirt-cheap valuation. The company has navigated the BPO industry’s changes with agility, shifting offshore to cut costs, layering in technology to differentiate, and securing marquee clients in growing sectors. Now, with legacy headwinds easing and new wins ramping up, IBEX is positioned to deliver solid growth on a much more profitable basis.

In the latest quarter, we saw the fruits of this strategy: record revenue and a 34% jump in EPS y/y. Management’s bold buybacks underscore their confidence that this performance is no fluke. IBEX is essentially saying it believes in itself.

At around $25 per share, the market is offering us a chance to own a quality business at around 5x forward EBITDA and 12x earnings—a valuation that implies little to no growth. But as we’ve detailed, growth is not only happening; it’s accelerating in the segments IBEX has cultivated. By this time next year, earnings are likely to be higher, the share count lower, and the company potentially re-rated closer to peers, resulting in a meaningfully higher stock price.

Could I be wrong? Sure—maybe AI displaces more human-led revenue than expected, or a client loss sets things back. But given IBEX’s asymmetric risk-reward, this is a risk I am willing to take.
